name: Qeemah
tagline: Cloud accounting and invoicing aimed at small businesses in the Gulf region, with Arabic and VAT handling.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: An agent can absolutely build you a ledger, an invoice generator, and a VAT summary in a weekend, and for a freelancer that is genuinely most of the job. Where it falls apart is the part nobody enjoys: tax authority e-invoicing rules, the exact XML or QR payload a regulator expects, and the audit trail that keeps you out of trouble. Regional accounting tools earn their money by tracking those rules as they change, which is a subscription problem rather than a coding problem. If your invoices need to be accepted by a tax portal, DIY is a bad idea. If you just need clean invoices, expenses, and a number to hand your accountant, DIY is fine.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app that stores customers, items, invoices and expenses, generates PDF invoices with tax lines, and produces a period tax and profit summary.
requirements: Node and a local database (SQLite is enough)
Your own tax rates and invoice numbering rules
An accountant to sanity check the output before you file anything
whatYouLose: Regulator-compliant e-invoicing output and whatever signing or QR format the tax authority currently demands
Rule updates when tax law or invoice formats change, which they do
Bank feeds, payment links, and payroll if the product offers them
Arabic and bilingual document layout that actually looks right, RTL PDFs are more annoying than they sound
Anyone to blame but yourself during an audit
moatNotes: The moat is regulatory drift plus localization, not features. Every rule change is a renewal reason.
whyPeopleStillPay: Accounting software is bought as insurance. The invoice you generate yourself might be arithmetically perfect and still get rejected by a tax portal because a field is missing or a signature format changed last quarter. Paying a regional vendor outsources the job of reading tax circulars and shipping updates, plus it gives your accountant something familiar to open. Nobody pays for the invoice PDF, they pay to not think about compliance.
notes: Fine as a freelancer bookkeeping build; do not use it as your filing system of record.
prompt:
Build a local-first small business bookkeeping and invoicing web app in an empty folder.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Next.js with the App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, schema created on first run by a migration script
- Zod for input validation
- PDF generation with Puppeteer rendering an HTML invoice template

Data model:
- Company profile: name, address, tax registration number, logo path, default currency, default tax rate
- Customers: name, address, tax number, email
- Items: name, unit price, tax rate
- Invoices: number, issue date, due date, customer, line items (description, qty, unit price, tax rate), subtotal, tax total, grand total, status (draft, sent, paid)
- Expenses: date, vendor, category, amount, tax amount, note, optional receipt file path

Features in scope:
- CRUD screens for customers, items, invoices, expenses
- Sequential invoice numbering with a configurable prefix, enforced at the database level
- Server-side computed totals, never trust client math, round tax per line to 2 decimals
- Invoice PDF download with a clean printable template that supports left-to-right and right-to-left layouts driven by a locale toggle (en, ar)
- Reports page: for a chosen date range show revenue, expenses, profit, output tax collected, input tax paid, net tax position, plus a per-customer revenue table
- CSV export of invoices and expenses
- Full JSON backup and restore

Explicitly out of scope: user accounts, multi-tenant support, cloud hosting, payment processing, bank feeds, payroll, telemetry, and any government e-invoicing submission or cryptographic invoice signing. Put a visible banner on the reports page reading that output is for personal bookkeeping and is not a filing-ready tax return.

Run it with npm run dev on localhost only, store the SQLite file and uploads under ./data, keep any config in .env with a committed .env.example, and write a README covering setup, backup, and the tax assumptions the code makes.
